value_chain_position: Data-center power & thermal-management equipment maker — sells UPS systems, switchgear, power distribution and liquid-cooling gear to hyperscalers/colos, the equipment layer of grid + AI-power buildout.
cost_curve_verified: This is an equipment maker with no output commodity, so the equivalent test is the price-versus-input-cost line: the screener's deterministic reading of a 34.4% gross margin and $1.58 billion of net debt is stale by two quarters and understates the company on both counts — the June-quarter gross margin was 37.7% and recomputed net debt at 30 June 2026 was $146 million including finance leases; the company-reported adjusted operating margin of 22.6% for the second quarter of 2026, up 410 basis points from a year earlier, confirms the direction, so the proxy agrees on direction and disagrees on level.
gm_trajectory: Gross margin expanded from 32.2% in the June 2025 quarter to 37.7% in the June 2026 quarter — about 550 basis points — while revenue in the same quarters grew 24%, from $2,638 million to $3,274 million; expanding margin on rising volume is pricing power, not volume bought with price.
bull_thesis:
Vertiv is the equipment layer of the artificial-intelligence build-out, and the evidence that it holds real pricing power is now on the income statement rather than in the script. In the June 2026 quarter revenue reached $3,274 million, up 24% from a year earlier, while gross margin widened from 32.2% to 37.7% and adjusted operating margin — profit from operations before one-off items, as a share of sales — rose 410 basis points to 22.6%. A company giving away price to fill factories does the opposite. Management then raised full-year 2026 guidance for the third time in six months, to roughly $14.0 billion of sales at the midpoint, 30-32% organic growth, adjusted earnings per share of $6.65-$6.75 and adjusted free cash flow of $2.4-$2.6 billion, and guided the September quarter to 34-36% organic growth. At the May 2026 investor conference in Greenville the company reset its five-year frame upward, to 20-22% annual revenue growth and a 27% adjusted operating margin ambition for 2030, with capital spending held to 3-4% of sales and cash conversion of 95-100%.

The order book behind that is contractual rather than aspirational. Backlog last disclosed at $15.0 billion on 11 February 2026 was more than double the prior year and 57% higher than the September 2025 quarter, on orders up 252% year on year and a book-to-bill ratio — orders taken divided by revenue billed — of 2.9 times. Management defines backlog tightly: 'a binding purchase order... very often with advanced payment.' That definition is corroborated in cash, not just words: June-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $925 million, up 234%, was driven substantially by customer deposits taken against those orders. Named, dated deployments back it up — Hut 8 and Compass Data Centers, a Naval Postgraduate School installation around NVIDIA's DGX GB300 announced 23 July 2026, VisionBay.ai with Foxconn in Taiwan, Data4 in Frankfurt.

The obsolescence question that recurs every quarter has so far resolved in Vertiv's favour. Analysts have asked in turn whether in-row heat exchangers, microfluidic chip cooling, 800-volt direct-current architectures or warmer-running chips would strip Vertiv's content out of the rack. The falsifiable answer is dollars of Vertiv equipment per megawatt of data centre, and that number has gone up, from a $3.0-3.5 million range to $3.25-3.75 million as of the September 2025 quarter. Vertiv is now embedded in NVIDIA's Omniverse DSX design blueprint (1 June 2026) and in its 800-volt reference architecture — a switching cost that deepens each design cycle rather than eroding.

Capital discipline is the quiet part of the case and it is unusually good. The company repurchased $599.9 million of its own stock in fiscal 2024, when the shares traded at a small fraction of today's price, and has bought back nothing in 2025 or 2026 at three to five times that level, redirecting cash to bolt-on acquisitions that extend the thermal portfolio (Great Lakes and WeiLay in 2025, ThermoKey completed 12 June 2026, Strategic Thermal Labs announced 20 July 2026). Net debt of $146 million including leases against trailing adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $2.52 billion means the balance sheet imposes no constraint at all; liquidity is $5.6 billion. Returns confirm it: return on invested capital of 20.8% and return on equity of 42.1%.

The conditions this case depends on are three. Europe must return to growth in the second half of 2026 after running down 29% organically in the March quarter, as guidance assumes. The June-quarter revenue shortfall must prove to be the timing shift management described rather than the start of a conversion problem on the new prefabricated systems. And hyperscaler capital spending must continue at the pace implied by the order book — the $15 billion backlog covers rather more than one year of sales, so a pause shows up late, not early.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require Vertiv to be a bad company. It requires only that the cycle turns and that the buyer, at today's price, has no early warning.

Start with what has been removed. From the 2026 reporting year Vertiv no longer discloses orders, order forecasts or backlog with quarterly results — announced in the June 2025 quarter, confirmed on the February 2026 call immediately after reporting the best order quarter in its history, and executed since. The June 2026 call gave no backlog figure and no book-to-bill ratio. The reasoning offered is that lumpy orders create 'unnecessary volatility... not beneficial to our investors.' Whatever the intent, the effect is that the single leading indicator for a business whose entire valuation rests on forward demand is now visible once a year, in the annual report. Every bullish claim about pipeline strength since February 2026 is unaudited management assertion.

Then look at what this company did the last time input costs ran ahead of a fixed-price order book. In fiscal 2022 revenue grew 13.8% while net income collapsed to $77 million and free cash flow turned to negative $264 million. Vertiv books binding purchase orders, often more than a year ahead of delivery, at prices struck today; copper, steel, transformers, switchgear components and freight are costs, so any inflation in them is a margin headwind, never a revenue tailwind. The 2025 tariff episode was a mild rerun — adjusted operating margin fell 110 basis points year on year in the June 2025 quarter, and the promise to be 'tariff neutral exiting 2025' slipped a quarter to the March 2026 quarter. The mechanism has been managed better; it has not been abolished.

The cracks in execution are new and they are in the strategically important part. June-quarter revenue of $3,274 million came in roughly 3% below what the street expected, attributed to 'multi-phase project execution and temporary supply chain dynamics' and a 'learning curve' on large interconnected projects. The converged, prefabricated products that justify the premium — OneCore and SmartRun — recognise revenue against project milestones, which is structurally lumpier and more working-capital hungry than shipping components. Organic growth in the quarter was 18%, down from 34% organic a year earlier, with five percentage points of the headline 24% coming from acquisitions and one from currency. Full-year guidance nonetheless calls for 30-32% organic, which requires a very sharp second-half reacceleration; the September-quarter guide of 34-36% organic is where that gets tested.

Europe is the clearest instance of narrative running ahead of numbers. Management called the region a 'coiled spring... uncoiling' in February 2026 while it ran down 14%, and it then ran down 29% organically in the March 2026 quarter. Guidance embeds a second-half return to growth that has not yet appeared.

Competition is not standing still. Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB, nVent, Johnson Controls and Carrier all attack parts of this stack, and liquid cooling in particular has attracted a crowd. The hyperscaler customers are among the most sophisticated procurement organisations on earth, they are vertically integrating where they can, and customer concentration in a business where single orders now move a quarter cuts both ways.

What confirms the bear case: a September or December quarter where organic growth undershoots the 34-36% guide; any sequential decline in gross margin on rising revenue, which would say price is being conceded; the fiscal 2026 annual report showing backlog below $15 billion; a hyperscaler publicly pausing or re-phasing a build; or free cash flow deteriorating as customer deposits unwind into deliveries without being replaced by new ones. Priced adversely, this is not a small drawdown. The shares traded at $118.70 within the past twelve months and fell about 25% in four weeks into the July 2026 report on a 3% revenue miss — the market has already demonstrated how fast it will re-rate this name when conversion is questioned.
sop_bull:
Favorable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately), built on fiscal 2027 estimated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, using the reported segment split of roughly 82% product and 18% service. Assumes revenue reaches about $17.4 billion in 2027 (the upper end of the company's 20-22% five-year growth frame plus completed acquisitions) at an adjusted operating margin of about 26%, giving roughly $4.83 billion of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.

Parts: (1) Service, about $3.2 billion of revenue at a 33% margin, or roughly $1.06 billion of earnings, valued at 28-34 times — a recurring, contracted maintenance and monitoring annuity attached to an installed base, which deserves a premium to the equipment multiple — take 34 times, giving about $36.0 billion, or $91.60 a share. (2) Product, about $14.2 billion of revenue at a 26.5% margin, or roughly $3.77 billion of earnings, valued at 30 times, giving about $113.1 billion, or $287.80 a share; 30 times is above where Eaton trades on trailing earnings (31.9 times) only in the sense that it is applied to a year further out, and is justified by 20%-plus organic growth against Eaton's high single digits. (3) Overlay: net debt of $146 million including finance leases, subtracted, worth about $0.40 a share.

Total: about $378 a share on roughly 393 million diluted shares. This is close to the twelve-month high of $379.94 and near the top of the published street range, and it requires both the 2027 revenue and the 2027 margin to land at the favourable end.
sop_bear:
Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the chain regime turns against Vertiv: hyperscaler capital spending enters a digestion phase, order intake stalls so the backlog converts without being replaced, the new capacity added through 2026 runs under-absorbed, and copper, steel and component inflation plus tariffs push against a fixed-price order book — the exact combination that took Vertiv's free cash flow to negative $264 million in fiscal 2022.

Parts: (1) Service, about $2.7 billion of revenue at a 30% margin, or roughly $0.81 billion of earnings, valued at 20 times — service holds up best because it is attached to equipment already installed — giving about $16.2 billion, or $41.20 a share. (2) Product, about $11.8 billion of revenue (roughly flat with 2026, so no growth at all) at a compressed 20.2% margin, or roughly $2.39 billion of earnings, valued at 14 times, giving about $33.5 billion, or $85.20 a share; 14 times is below where Hubbell trades today (21.4 times) because a stalled Vertiv would be re-rated as a cyclical equipment maker that has just lost its growth premium, not as a secular compounder. (3) Overlay: net debt of $146 million subtracted, about $0.40 a share. There is no structural floor to add — the dividend of $0.0625 a quarter and the small net cash position are immaterial at this size, and the unsolicited $410 mini-tender the company told shareholders to reject on 15 May 2026 is conditioned on the shares trading above $410 and is therefore not a floor of any kind.

Total: about $128 a share. That is a severe number, but it sits just above the $118.70 low printed within the past twelve months, so it is a level this market has already visited rather than a theoretical construct.
sop_breakdown: Base case, built on fiscal 2027 estimated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $4.62 billion — revenue of roughly $16.9 billion (21% growth on the $14.0 billion guided for 2026) at an adjusted operating margin of about 25.5%, part-way between the 23.8% guided for 2026 and the 27% the company targets for 2030. Service, about $3.1 billion of revenue at a 33% margin, or $1.03 billion of earnings, at 30 times = $30.9 billion, or $78.60 a share. Product, about $13.8 billion of revenue at a 26% margin, or $3.59 billion of earnings, at 26 times = $93.3 billion, or $237.40 a share. Less net debt of $146 million including finance leases, about $0.40 a share. Total roughly $124 billion of equity value on about 393 million diluted shares, or $315 a share. Sense-check: that is about 36 times estimated 2027 adjusted earnings per share of roughly $8.70, and about 27 times estimated 2027 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — a full price justified only by the growth rate, and deliberately below the street's $357 consensus and $355 median.
risk_reward: Levels, not ratios. The shares trade at $273.35. The base-case sum-of-the-parts value is $315, so the upside to fair value is about $42 a share. The adverse case is $128, so the downside if the order cycle turns is about $145 a share. There is no structural floor beneath the price — no deal terms, no meaningful net cash per share, no tender to lean on. The asymmetry is therefore against the buyer at today's level: roughly three and a half times as much room below as above. At about $215 — a level this stock printed nine days ago, on 29-30 July 2026 — the same two anchors give roughly $100 of upside against roughly $87 of downside, and the arithmetic turns favourable.
catalyst_status_note: Both load-bearing events have already happened. The May 19-20 2026 investor conference in Greenville, South Carolina reset the five-year frame upward, to 20-22% annual revenue growth and a 27% adjusted operating margin ambition for 2030. The second-quarter 2026 results, published before the market opened on 29 July 2026, delivered adjusted earnings per share of $1.52 (up 60%), adjusted operating margin of 22.6% (up 410 basis points) and the third increase to full-year guidance in six months, to roughly $14.0 billion of sales and $6.65-$6.75 of adjusted earnings per share. The market's reaction is also spent in both directions: the shares fell about 25% over the four weeks into that print on a roughly 3% revenue shortfall, then recovered from about $222 on 30 July to $273.35 today. In this lane the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict — it is neither a credit nor a penalty.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the business — it is about what the market is currently choosing to look at.

The street's error in July was arithmetic on the wrong line. Analysts sold a 3% revenue shortfall in the June quarter ($3,274 million against expectations near $3,375 million) while adjusted operating margin expanded 410 basis points, adjusted earnings per share grew 60%, adjusted free cash flow tripled to $925 million and full-year guidance went up across every line. Several published notes in the days after made exactly that point. On this narrow question the sellers were wrong and the stock has already taken back most of the ground — from about $222 on 30 July to $273.35 on 4 August, a gain of roughly 23% in four sessions.

Our disagreement is with the reflex that followed. The bullish restatement now settles on two figures that are no longer current: a $15 billion backlog and a book-to-bill ratio of 2.9 times. Both are true as of 11 February 2026 and neither has been refreshed since, because Vertiv discontinued quarterly orders and backlog disclosure from the 2026 reporting year. Notes written in the last week still quote them as though they describe today. They do not; they describe a quarter that closed more than seven months ago. The market is extrapolating a demand signal it can no longer observe.

The second street assumption we would challenge is that the mix of growth does not matter. Headline growth of 24% in the June quarter contained 18% organic, five points from acquisitions and one from currency, against 34% organic in the same quarter a year earlier. Full-year guidance still calls for 30-32% organic, and the September quarter is guided to 34-36% organic. That is a very steep second-half reacceleration to underwrite from a base that just decelerated, and it depends in part on Europe reversing from down 29% organically in the March quarter to growth — a turn management has been describing as imminent since February while the number went the other way.

Where we agree with the bulls, and against the bears, is on obsolescence. The recurring worry that in-row heat exchangers, microfluidics, 800-volt direct current or warmer-running chips will strip Vertiv's content out of the rack is testable, and the test has come back the other way: dollars of Vertiv content per megawatt has been guided up, not down, and the company sits inside NVIDIA's reference architecture and design blueprint. The risk here is cyclical, not structural, and much of the bearish commentary confuses the two.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash crisis in this name and it would be dishonest to invent one. Net debt is $146 million including finance leases against roughly $2.52 billion of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, liquidity is $5.6 billion, there is no maturity wall, and free cash flow is guided at $2.4-$2.6 billion for 2026. The risk over the next three to nine months is entirely to the share price and to the growth narrative, not to solvency.

Three specific hazards. First, the September-quarter print, expected in late October 2026, carries a guide of 34-36% organic growth and $1.77-$1.83 of adjusted earnings per share. That is the steepest organic bar the company has set, it comes immediately after a quarter that missed on revenue for execution reasons, and it must be cleared with new capacity in Malaysia and Italy still ramping. A repeat timing shift would be read very differently the second time.

Second, the working-capital shape of the new business. June-quarter free cash flow of $925 million, up 234%, was substantially driven by customer deposits and advance payments taken against orders. The chief financial officer said plainly in April 2026 that deposits are 'a way to look at backlog, but it's not entirely our read through.' Deposits flatter cash while orders are being taken and reverse as those orders are delivered. If order intake merely slows — it need not fall — the cash-flow line can deteriorate sharply while the income statement still looks fine, and that would arrive before any backlog disclosure could explain it. Capital spending is simultaneously stepping to about 4% of 2026 sales, roughly $560 million against $226 million spent in 2025.

Third, input costs and tariffs. Vertiv books binding purchase orders, often more than a year ahead of delivery, at prices struck today. Copper, steel, transformers and freight are costs to this business, so any inflation in them squeezes a fixed-price order book — and management has been explicit that it operates in 'what remains an inflationary environment', with the tariff perimeter still shifting under Sections 122 and 232. The company's own fiscal 2022, when revenue grew 13.8% while free cash flow went to negative $264 million, is the precedent for how quickly this can bite.

The fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 report, due around February 2027, brings a different kind of hazard: the annual report is now the only place the backlog figure appears.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling episode largely happened, and it happened nine days ago. Vertiv fell about 25% over four weeks into the 29 July 2026 report — a decline driven by momentum and thematic artificial-intelligence funds de-risking rather than by anything in the accounts — and the low print around $222 on 30 July was reclaimed within four sessions, with the shares at $273.35 today and up about 3.9% on the day. Zacks moved the name to its top rank on 3 August and several sell-side notes published between 30 July and 3 August framed the drop as a misreading.

That sequence tells you the shareholder base here is fast, not sticky. This is not a yield-oriented or income register that would be mechanically forced out by a distribution change — the dividend is a token $0.0625 a quarter and no one owns Vertiv for it. It is a growth and momentum register, heavily represented in artificial-intelligence thematic products and index funds, whose selling is triggered by trend breaks and earnings-revision breaks rather than by valuation. Institutional flow in the screener reads a neutral 52 out of 100, and the most recent large holder movement disclosed is Bank of America reducing by about 814,000 shares.

The practical consequence: there is no structural overhang waiting to clear, and equally no patient base to cushion the next disappointment. A single quarter of organic growth below the guided 34-36% would produce the same mechanical de-risking again, from a higher starting price. Insiders will not be the counterweight — there have been no open-market purchases against 38 disposals totalling about 271,000 shares, and the recent Form 4 filings are dividend-equivalent accruals and tax withholding on vesting rather than conviction sales or buys.
forcing_function:
Three dated events, in order of consequence.

The third-quarter 2026 results, expected in late October 2026, are the real test. Management has guided that quarter to $3,650-$3,850 million of sales, 34-36% organic growth and $1.77-$1.83 of adjusted earnings per share. Because orders and backlog are no longer disclosed quarterly, the reported revenue line is now the only observable proof that the order book is converting on schedule — it has been promoted, by the company's own disclosure choice, from a routine number into the whole thesis. Clearing 34-36% organic after a quarter that slipped on 'multi-phase project execution' would settle the question; missing it twice in a row would not be forgiven as timing.

The same report carries the second half of the European promise. Guidance embeds a return to year-on-year growth in Europe, the Middle East and Africa in the second half of 2026, after that region ran down 29% organically in the March 2026 quarter and down 14% in the December 2025 quarter. This is the oldest unverified claim in the file.

The fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, expected around February 2027, bring the annual report and with it the only backlog figure investors will see all year — the first opportunity since 11 February 2026 to check the $15 billion against something the company must file rather than merely assert.

One further event is not in Vertiv's control and matters more than any of them: the capital-spending guidance issued by the major cloud operators through their own reporting seasons. Vertiv is a derivative of that number, and it will re-rate on their disclosures before it re-rates on its own.
peer_comps_note: Against the assigned competitor set, Vertiv is the most expensive name in the group on trailing figures and roughly in line once you credit its growth. On enterprise value to trailing twelve-month earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: Vertiv 41.9 times, Eaton 31.9 times, Johnson Controls 28.2 times, nVent 27.6 times, Carrier 23.7 times, Hubbell 21.4 times. On our 2027 estimate of about $4.62 billion, Vertiv falls to roughly 23 times — inside the peer band — but only if that estimate lands. The growth gap justifies part of the premium: Vertiv guided 30-32% organic growth for 2026 against high single digits to low double digits for most of this group, and it is the only one carrying essentially no net debt (0.06 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, against 3.4 times at Eaton and Hubbell and 4.0 times at Carrier). It also earns materially better returns — 20.8% on invested capital against 9-11% across the group. The multiples used in our base case, 26 times for the equipment business and 30 times for services, therefore sit above the peer median by design; they are not defensible if growth normalises toward peer rates, which is precisely what the adverse case prices. Note that the two European competitors in the assigned set, ABB and Schneider Electric, were not priced for this comparison, so the read rests on the five North American names.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business at a price that leaves the buyer holding the wrong end of the asymmetry, so the answer is to wait for the wash-out rather than buy now — and to name the level rather than wave at one.

What is genuinely strong. The pricing-power test passes cleanly: gross margin widened about 550 basis points, from 32.2% to 37.7%, over the year to the June 2026 quarter while revenue grew 24%. Expanding margin on rising volume in a supply-constrained niche is the honest signature of pricing power; the opposite pattern would have told us volume was being bought with price. Adjusted operating margin rose 410 basis points to 22.6% and management raised full-year guidance for the third time in six months. The forensic record supports taking that at face value — seven earnings beats in seven quarters, free cash flow guided to $1.4 billion for 2025 and delivered at $1.89 billion, and, most tellingly, $599.9 million of stock repurchased in 2024 near the lows and nothing repurchased in 2025 or 2026 at three to five times the price. Buying low and declining to buy high is the reverse of what most management teams do with a hot share price, and it is the single best piece of evidence on capital discipline in the file. The balance sheet imposes no constraint at all: $146 million of net debt including leases against about $2.52 billion of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, with $5.6 billion of liquidity. Returns are rising, not falling — 20.8% on invested capital, 42.1% on equity — which is why we read the moat as narrow but widening rather than wide or eroding. And the terminal-value question is benign: artificial intelligence is this company's demand driver, not its displacer.

What holds us back, in order. First, the price. Our base-case sum-of-the-parts value is $315 a share against $273.35 today — about 15% of upside, and that already assumes 2027 revenue of roughly $16.9 billion at a 25.5% adjusted operating margin, which is not a conservative set of inputs. We are deliberately below the street's $357 consensus. Against that modest upside sits an adverse case at $128, built on the order book converting without being replaced and margin compressing under input costs and under-absorbed new capacity. That number is not theoretical: this stock printed $118.70 within the past twelve months, and fiscal 2022 shows what this business looks like when input costs run ahead of a fixed-price order book — revenue up 13.8%, net income $77 million, free cash flow negative $264 million. Roughly $42 of upside against roughly $145 of downside is not a shape we pay up for.

Second, the instrument panel has been removed. From the 2026 reporting year Vertiv no longer publishes orders or backlog quarterly. The $15 billion backlog and 2.9 times book-to-bill that the bullish commentary still quotes were last disclosed on 11 February 2026 and describe a quarter that closed more than seven months ago. Management pre-announced the change before the blowout, which is mitigating, and the stated rationale about lumpiness is coherent. The effect is not mitigated at all: the leading indicator that would tell us when this cycle turns is now visible once a year. That is a real reason to demand a wider margin of safety, not a smaller one.

Third, two live operating claims are unproven. Europe must swing from down 29% organically in the March quarter to growth in the second half of 2026, a turn management has been calling imminent since February while the number deteriorated. And the September quarter must deliver 34-36% organic growth immediately after a quarter that slipped 3% on what was described as a learning curve on large interconnected projects — the first time the converged, prefabricated strategy that justifies the premium has cost the company a number.

On timing: the forced selling already happened. The shares fell about 25% over four weeks into 29 July and have taken back roughly 23% in the four sessions since, closing at $273.35 today. Buying here is chasing the recovery, not the wash-out. The level we want is about $215 — printed nine days ago, on 29-30 July 2026 — where the same base case offers roughly $100 of upside against roughly $87 of downside and the arithmetic inverts. Failing that, a September-quarter print that clears 34-36% organic growth with Europe positive would let us raise the base case and justify paying closer to today's price on better information.

The value score sits at the same level as the execution call, and for once that is not a default: the discount to our own fair value is thin at 15%, and while the forensic quality is high and the moat is widening rather than melting, neither of those creates value at a price that has already been paid. Both scores are held at neutral. The catalyst position — that the investor conference and the June-quarter print have both already fired — carries no weight either way in this lane; dated-event asymmetry is another book's business, and a spent event on a clean franchise is neither a credit nor a penalty here.
